_about: Each entry puts one known bug back into internal/config and the suite must fail. The set is deliberately about the aliasing invariant, because that invariant has been written down twice and violated twice: once by an element write through a shared array, once by an append into shared spare capacity. A comment restating a rule is not a regression test. See scripts/mutate.py for what the run checks and what equivalent means. Run: make mutate

mutants.old:
c.RemoveOverride(o.Username)
	// appended, never an append into c.Overrides:
mutants.new: // appended, never an append into c.Overrides:
mutants.note: the removal moved after the append by deletion of the pre-append call; paired with CG6, which moves it after explicitly. This one is the 'removal dropped entirely' shape: an amend then leaves two entries for one child and which grant wins depends on order.
appended writing into the caller's own array instead of the fresh one; out stays used by the copy above, so this compiles and only the aliasing changes.
the UpsertProfile add path appends into an array another Config still holds, so a's saved document gains b's new profile
the UpsertUser add path appends into an array another Config still holds, so a's saved document enforces an account a never assigned
the flag never survives decoding, so every rule is an ordinary one and an all-day parent loses the last minute anyway
an all-day rule is asked for clock ends it does not have, so a form that clears them is refused
the all-day rule that left 08:00 in both boxes is rejected as the typo it is not

mutants.old: so the window is empty and enforces nothing; for a rule with no minute free set allDay instead
mutants.new: so the window is empty and enforces nothing; write 00:00 to 23:59 for an all-day rule
mutants.note: the message recommends the 1439-minute window again, which is the advice this issue exists to retire

ProfileFor hands a switched-off account its profile back. The daemon still does not lock that account, because enforce.go tests the switch before it ever asks for a profile -- the two checks are redundant on purpose and each alone holds the line, which is why no single mutant here is a live fail-open. What this pins is the helper's contract, the one the web layer and the dashboard also call: no set in the repo had a mutant touching Enabled anywhere. TestUserForAndProfileFor.

the profile-name ceiling stops biting. The document is then bounded only by the request body limit while the enforcement loop re-decodes it every 30 seconds, and #147's overflow-wrap rule becomes the only thing standing between one long string and a broken layout. Killed by the table case in TestValidateRejectsEachMalformedField and by TestTheNameCeilingIsEnforcedOnTheEditPathToo, which is the half that matters most: with the ceiling gone from config, `plock profile edit` writes what the web page refuses, which is the drift #127 was about.

the rule-name half of the same ceiling, removed on its own. A rule name is quoted by the audit trail and rendered as a row header on /profiles, and `plock rule add` reaches it without going through any form. The two checks are separate statements with separate messages, so one can be deleted while the other still passes every test that only exercises profiles.

bytes instead of characters, on the profile name. This is the mutant an ASCII suite cannot see: 200 `n`s are 200 bytes, so every other case still passes. TestTheNameCeilingIsCharactersNotBytes hands it 200 two-byte characters — over the ceiling in bytes, exactly at it in runes — because counting bytes would refuse every accented name a household actually writes while accepting 200 repetitions of one letter, which is the opposite of what the ceiling is for.

the same unit error on the rule name. Named separately from CG17 because the two statements are independent: converting one and not the other leaves a document where a profile name is counted in characters and a rule name in bytes, and no test that uses only ASCII would notice either half.
